nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_source.description: Real-world traffic video frames from which vehicle locations are extracted and reformed as position matrices, used as inputs for the DRL method.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Available from the corresponding author upon request; no public link or DOI provided.

nodes_source.source_quote: The simulation parameters regarding driving behaviors are calibrated based on empirical data.
nodes_source.description: Data used to calibrate the simulation parameters for driving behaviors in the SUMO microscopic traffic simulator.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: No information on availability, source, or URL provided.

nodes_process.node_name: Extract vehicle locations and form position matrices
nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames and then reformed into position matrices. These matrices represent the traffic state at a given time step. The control area size is X x Y.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=2, no tools named, control_area_size mentioned but no specific values.

nodes_process.node_name: Stack and down-sample position matrices for state
nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state s₁: S₁ = {m₁-(N-1),..., m₁}.
nodes_process.description: Position matrices from N consecutive time steps are stacked to form the traffic state representation. Down-sampling is applied to reduce input dimensions while retaining vehicle position information, improving computational efficiency.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, no tools named, N stated, down_sampling_factor not.

nodes_process.node_name: Define reward function for ramp metering
nodes_process.source_quote: The reward r₁ after action at is defined by the following: rt = vt + wqt, μ > 0, ω < 0
nodes_process.description: The reward function `rt` is defined based on the average speed in the merging area (`vt`) and the average queue length at the on-ramp (`qt`) during time steps `t` and `t+1`. Positive `mu` and negative `omega` are weights to balance vehicle mobility and reduce delays.

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: A deep neural network, termed Q-network, approximates Q*(s,a). It's a revised version of Mnih et al.'s Q-network, comprising three CNN layers and one FC layer per output. A multitask learning strategy extends the FC layer to predict speed and queue length simultaneously.

nodes_process.node_name: Train Deep Q-learning for ramp metering
nodes_process.source_quote: The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1. The ramp meter takes new action with the e-greedy strategy, meaning that the agent does not always adopt the best action derived from current Q (s, a, w).
nodes_process.description: The Q-network is trained using Adam to minimize a combined loss function. Training incorporates experience replay and a target network for stability, and uses an epsilon-greedy strategy for action selection to balance exploration and exploitation.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, Adam and SUMO mentioned, 7/8 parameters stated (number_of_training_episodes_N missing).

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31].
nodes_process.description: The simulation environment is set up using SUMO. It models a freeway connecting Qingdao and Huangdao, including a one-lane on-ramp and a three-lane mainline. Speed limits are 80 km/h for mainline and 40 km/h for on-ramp. Simulation runs from 7:50 a.m. to 9:00 a.m.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, SUMO mentioned, all parameters stated, but empirical data for calibration details are missing.

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network is trained in 10^6 training frames, and each scenario is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments.
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is evaluated in the SUMO simulation environment. Each scenario is run for 20 simulation experiments, with different random seeds. Evaluation metrics include travel times, queue lengths, and traffic flows.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no specific tools mentioned, number of experiments stated, random seed values not provided.

nodes_process.source_quote: the second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method. The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA method is implemented as a baseline. It fixes green phase length and determines red phase length based on previous red phase length and downstream occupancies. The ramp metering rate `rk` is calculated using `rk = rk-1 + KR[ok - ô] - Kp[ok-1 - ok]`.

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering
nodes_process.description: A baseline scenario without any ramp metering control is evaluated in the simulation environment to provide a reference for the DRL and PI-ALINEA methods.

nodes_process.node_name: Compare travel times, queue lengths, traffic flows
nodes_process.source_quote: The results demonstrate that, in comparison with a state-of-the-practice method, the proposed DRL method results in (1) lower travel times in the mainline, (2) shorter vehicle queues at the on-ramp, and (3) higher traffic flows downstream of the merging area.
nodes_process.description: The performance of the DRL method, PI-ALINEA method, and no-control scenario are compared based on mean travel times, queue lengths at the on-ramp, and traffic flows downstream of the merging area. Results are presented in tables and figures.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no specific tools mentioned for visualization/comparison.

nodes_process.node_name: Conduct perturbation analysis on video data
nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. As shown in Figure 15, the control area is divided into eight subareas.
nodes_process.description: A perturbation analysis evaluates the impact of information from different video data subareas. The control area is divided into eight subareas, and information from specific subareas is removed from the original data to generate perturbed data. The DRL model is then evaluated with this perturbed data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, no tools mentioned, perturbation mechanism not fully detailed.
